plan.title: Why Costco's $1.50 Hot Dog Explains Its Whole Business
plan.description:
Costco has sold its hot dog combo for $1.50 since 1985, and that tiny price explains its entire business. Using Costco's fiscal 2025 annual report, we show how membership fees, razor-thin margins and 90%+ renewal rates power the machine.

Chapters:
0:00 The $1.50 hot dog
0:54 The $65 ticket
1:51 Selling at almost no profit
2:39 The loyalty machine
3:22 The upgrade
3:51 Less is more
4:30 The flywheel

Sources:

segments.narration: Since 1985, Costco has sold a hot dog and a soda for a dollar fifty.
Not a dollar fifty in 1985 money. A dollar fifty today. Forty years of inflation, and the price hasn't moved.
A Costco executive once told founder Jim Sinegal that the hot dog was losing money.
His reported answer? Raise the price of that hot dog and I will kill you. Figure it out.
That sounds like terrible business. Until you realise Costco isn't really in the hot dog business.
It isn't really in the grocery business either.
Last year it sold almost two hundred and seventy billion dollars of stuff.
And the profit on all those products? Surprisingly thin.
Because the real money is hiding somewhere else. In your wallet. In one small plastic card.
This is how Costco really makes money.
To shop at Costco, you first have to pay just to walk through the door.
A basic Gold Star membership in the United States costs sixty five dollars a year.
That sounds small. Now multiply it.
At the end of fiscal 2025, Costco had about eighty one million paid memberships.
Together, those fees brought in about five point three billion dollars in a single year.
Hold that number in your head. Because here's the twist.
Costco's total profit for the year, after paying for absolutely everything, was about eight point one billion dollars.
Five point three billion in fees. Eight point one billion in profit.
The fees alone are worth about two thirds of the entire company's profit.
And a fee costs almost nothing to collect. No pallets. No trucks. No shelf space.
Almost every dollar of it drops straight to the bottom line.
So what's happening inside the store? This is where it gets strange.
Costco's gross margin in 2025 was about eleven percent.
In plain words, sell a hundred dollars of goods, and only about eleven dollars is left after paying for the goods themselves.
And those eleven dollars still have to pay for the workers, the rent, the electricity and the trucks.
Most supermarkets keep a bigger slice than that.
Costco keeps its slice thin on purpose.
Thin margins mean low prices. And low prices make the card feel worth every cent.
Which is exactly why the hot dog stays at a dollar fifty.
It's not a meal. It's a reminder. Every visit, you see proof that the membership pays for itself.
But a membership is only valuable if people keep paying for it.
So how many actually come back?
In the United States and Canada, about ninety two percent of members renewed in 2025.
Worldwide, it was close to ninety percent.
Nine out of ten customers, paying again, every single year.
Plenty of gyms and streaming services would love to keep customers like that.
And here's the real test.
On the first of September 2024, Costco raised its membership fees in the United States and Canada.
Renewal rates still stayed above ninety percent.
When you raise your price and almost nobody leaves, customers are telling you they see real value.
Then there's the upgrade most shoppers don't think twice about.
The Executive membership costs another sixty five dollars on top. A hundred and thirty in total.
In return, members earn a cash reward on what they spend.
About thirty eight point seven million members chose it. That's close to half of all paid members.
Double the fee. And a reason to shop more often, because every trip earns a little back.
The last piece is something you notice the moment you walk in. There isn't much choice.
A typical Costco warehouse carries fewer than four thousand active products.
A regular supermarket can carry tens of thousands.
Fewer products means Costco buys each one in enormous volume.
And enormous volume means real power when it sits down with suppliers.
The buildings help too. Concrete floors. Goods stacked on pallets. No fancy displays.
Then there's Kirkland Signature, Costco's own brand, which the company calls a growing part of its sales.
One more thing you can only get by renewing that card.
So let's put the whole machine together.
Step one. Charge a yearly fee.
Step two. Use that money to keep prices so low the store barely profits on the goods.
Step three. Keep the range small, buy in huge volume, and run lean warehouses.
Step four. Members feel they save more than the fee, so nine in ten come back.
And the loop starts all over again.
That's how Costco sells close to two hundred and seventy billion dollars of goods on razor thin margins, and still earns around eight billion in profit.
The hot dog was never the product. Neither were the TVs, or the giant packs of toilet paper.
The product is the card. And everything inside the warehouse exists to make you renew it.
